common_name: Dutch Master Daffodil (Classic Golden-Yellow Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Dutch Master is a classic large trumpet daffodil, one of the earliest and most vigorous golden-yellow trumpet cultivars in commerce.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Dutch Master bears the classic large, solid golden-yellow trumpet form most people picture when they think of a daffodil, opening early in the spring season on sturdy stems that hold up well to wind and rain. Its vigor and reliability have made it one of the most widely planted trumpet daffodils for mass naturalizing in lawns, orchards, and woodland edges. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Tahiti is a long-standing double daffodil cultivar mixing yellow petals with orange-red segments.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Tahiti bears fully double blooms mixing rich yellow petals with segments of vivid orange-red, giving each flower a ruffled, layered look quite different from the simple trumpet-and-perianth form of most daffodils. It has remained in commerce for decades thanks to its warm, cheerful color combination and reliable performance in the garden. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

common_name: Barrett Browning Daffodil (Early White-and-Orange Small-Cup Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Barrett Browning is an early-blooming small-cup daffodil with a strong white-and-orange contrast.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Barrett Browning bears crisp white petals surrounding a small, frilled orange-red cup, a bold contrast held on sturdy stems that open among the earliest daffodils each spring. Its early bloom timing and reliable performance have kept it a garden favorite for mass plantings and naturalizing. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; introduced in 1923, Fortune is a historic large-cup daffodil that has remained popular for a full century.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Introduced in 1923, Fortune bears a clear yellow perianth surrounding a large, ruffled orange-red cup, a bold combination that helped make it one of the most influential and widely planted large-cup daffodils of the 20th century and a parent behind many later orange-cupped cultivars. Its century of continuous popularity is a testament to reliable, vigorous garden performance. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

common_name: Headbourne Hybrids Agapanthus (Hardy Blue-to-Violet Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Headbourne Hybrids is a deciduous, notably cold-hardy strain bred in England specifically to survive harsher winters than most agapanthus.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Headbourne Hybrids is a deciduous strain of agapanthus bred at Headbourne Worthy in England specifically to combine cold hardiness with the classic rounded umbels of blue, violet, and occasionally white flowers held on sturdy scapes above strap-shaped foliage. Unlike evergreen agapanthus, it dies back to the ground each winter, which is part of what allows it to survive colder climates than most agapanthus cultivars tolerate. Like other agapanthus it is drought-tolerant once established and blooms best when slightly pot-bound or crowded, so avoid dividing established clumps too frequently.

common_name: Snowball Agapanthus (Dwarf White Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Snowball is a compact white-flowered agapanthus selection well suited to containers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Snowball bears dense, rounded, pure white flower heads on compact scapes above narrow, dark-green strap leaves, offering a crisp, clean alternative to the blue and violet tones typical of most agapanthus. Its dwarf habit fits neatly into containers, border edges, or smaller garden spaces where larger agapanthus cultivars would be too imposing. Like other agapanthus it is drought-tolerant once established and blooms best when slightly pot-bound, so avoid dividing established clumps too frequently.

common_name: Twister Agapanthus (White Petals Edged in Blue Bicolor)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Twister is a distinctive bicolor agapanthus with blue-edged white petals.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Twister bears rounded umbels of white flowers each finely edged in blue, an unusual bicolor pattern that gives the flower heads a frosted, two-toned look at a distance, distinct from both solid white and solid blue agapanthus. It flowers in summer above clumps of narrow, dark green strap foliage and combines well with either pure blue or pure white companions in a mixed border. Like other agapanthus it is drought-tolerant once established and blooms best when slightly pot-bound, so avoid dividing established clumps too frequently.

common_name: Black Pantha Agapanthus (Very Dark Purple-Black Bud Dwarf Agapanthus)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Black Pantha is a dwarf agapanthus selection with unusually dark, near-black buds opening to deep purple flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Black Pantha bears striking near-black buds that open into densely packed umbels of deep purple flowers, among the darkest coloring available in agapanthus, on a compact, dwarf plant well suited to containers or the front of a border. Its dramatic bud color provides ornamental interest even before the flowers fully open. Like other agapanthus it is drought-tolerant once established and blooms best when slightly pot-bound, so avoid dividing established clumps too frequently.

common_name: Northern Star Agapanthus (Deep Blue Floriferous Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Northern Star is a floriferous deep-blue agapanthus with sturdy upright stems.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Northern Star bears an unusually heavy crop of deep blue flower heads on sturdy, upright scapes that hold well through wind and rain, blooming reliably above clumps of narrow strap foliage each summer. Its strong flowering performance makes it a good choice for mass plantings where consistent, abundant bloom matters more than novelty coloring. Like other agapanthus it is drought-tolerant once established and blooms best when slightly pot-bound, so avoid dividing established clumps too frequently.

common_name: Silver Moon Agapanthus (Cream-Edged Variegated Foliage Agapanthus)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Silver Moon is grown as much for its cream-variegated foliage as for its blue flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, with some afternoon shade helping to prevent leaf scorch on the variegated foliage in the hottest climates. Silver Moon carries strap-shaped leaves edged in creamy white year-round, providing ornamental interest well beyond its summer show of blue flower umbels, making it a good textural accent even out of bloom. Its variegation is most vivid in bright but not scorching light. Like other agapanthus it is drought-tolerant once established and blooms best when slightly pot-bound, so avoid dividing established clumps too frequently.

common_name: Mrs. Sinkins Dianthus (Fragrant Double White Heirloom Cottage Pink)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Mrs. Sinkins is a Victorian-era heirloom cottage pink prized for its powerful clove fragrance.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Mrs. Sinkins is a classic Victorian cottage pink, its fully double, fringed white flowers so densely petaled that the buds sometimes split open, carrying an intense, sweet clove fragrance widely regarded as one of the strongest of any dianthus. It forms a low mat of gray-green foliage that stays attractive between bloom flushes, and while its heavy flowers can be less weatherproof than modern hybrids, its scent and long garden history keep it in demand among heirloom plant collectors. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to keep the foliage mat dense and encourage a possible second flush.

common_name: Sops in Wine Dianthus (Maroon-and-White Fringed Heirloom Pink)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Sops in Wine is an old English cottage pink historically used to flavor wine and ale.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Sops in Wine is an old English heirloom cottage pink bearing deep maroon-red petals with a white base, each finely fringed along the edge, and carries the traditional clove fragrance the species is named for; historically the flowers were steeped in wine and ale to add flavor and color, giving the cultivar its name. It forms a low, tidy mat of gray-green foliage that stays attractive between bloom flushes. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to keep the foliage mat dense and encourage a possible second flush.

common_name: Doris Dianthus (Salmon-Pink Fragrant Long-Blooming Border Carnation)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Doris is a long-blooming border carnation hybrid valued for its long flowering season.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Doris bears fully double, salmon-pink flowers with a darker rose-pink eye and the classic sweet clove fragrance of dianthus, opening over an unusually long season from late spring well into fall with regular deadheading. As a border carnation type it grows a bit taller and more upright than low, mat-forming cheddar pinks, making it useful as a middle-of-the-border filler as well as an edging plant. Shear lightly after the main flush and deadhead through summer to keep flowers coming.

common_name: William Sim Dianthus (Foundation Scarlet Florist Carnation)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; William Sim is the historic foundation parent behind the modern florist Sim carnation line grown commercially worldwide.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. William Sim bears single, vivid scarlet-red flowers on tall, sturdy stems, and while less commonly grown as a garden plant today, it holds a special place in horticultural history as the foundation parent behind the entire modern line of Sim-type florist carnations grown commercially around the world for the cut-flower trade. In the garden it performs like other carnations, benefiting from sharp drainage and full sun, and rewarding with the classic sweet clove fragrance of the species. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage continued bloom and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Tiny Rubies Dianthus (Miniature Double Rose-Pink Cheddar Pink)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; Tiny Rubies is a miniature cheddar pink forming a very dense, low mat.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Tiny Rubies forms an exceptionally dense, low mat of fine, silvery-blue foliage smothered each spring in tiny, fully double, rose-pink flowers, its miniature scale making it well suited to rock gardens, gravel paths, and the edges of stone walls where larger dianthus would look out of proportion. Like other cheddar pinks it thrives in lean, sharply drained, rocky-to-sandy soil and shows good heat tolerance compared to alpine dianthus species. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to keep the mat dense and tidy through the rest of the season.

common_name: Sooty Dianthus (Dark Chocolate Foliage with Near-Black Crimson Flowers)

planting.note: Direct sow or plant transplants in fall for spring bloom in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Sooty is a Victorian-era Sweet William cultivar grown as much for its near-black foliage as its flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Sooty is a striking Victorian heirloom Sweet William grown as much for its dark, chocolate-maroon foliage as for its clusters of small, near-black crimson flowers, a dramatically dark color combination unusual among garden dianthus and useful for adding contrast next to silver or chartreuse companions. Sweet William is technically a short-lived biennial or short-lived perennial, often grown as a biennial sown one year to bloom the next, and it self-sows readily where happy. Deadhead spent flower clusters to extend bloom and prevent excessive self-seeding if a tidier planting is desired.
